title: The Winging of the Man of Peace
english: He was handed over, and having gone away, he approached with life as a burden. All my enemies were whispering against me; none of them spoke against me with boldness. And you find the Jews seeking how they might take him secretly; they were whispering to Judas, and he to them; for he did not enter a synagogue and shout this: 'What do you want to give me, and I will hand him over to you?' (Matt 26:14-15). Indeed, they themselves did not come to seize him for forty days.

This is what Jesus himself says: 'I teach every day' (Matt 26:21) in the synagogue, and now 'as if I had come to a robber.' They set a lawless word against me. They were reading the Scriptures 'every Sabbath' so that they might learn the things of the law. And from the opposite, it was necessary for those reading with the law to know who is the one prophesied and testified to by the Scriptures; they set a lawless word against me, saying: 'This one does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub.' 'If this man were from God, he would not have loosed the Sabbath' (John 11:45). 'Is it not bad that we say, "You are a Samaritan and have a demon"?' This is the one against whom they set a lawless word. And it is possible, since even in the legal briefs 'he set' is often taken; voices were set against Pilate concerning him.

Does he who is sleeping not add to rising? Rather, he himself says: since death surrounded me, I slept; for in the Scriptures the name of sleep sometimes signifies death. Sleep is also called slumber, and the union of a man with a woman is called sleep. And death is also called sleep according to the Scripture because of the expectation of the resurrection; for just as he who sleeps, if he suffers no harm to nature, might be raised, so the dying man will be raised. Thus indeed it is said, 'all shall sleep,' and, 'I do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who have slept' (Acts 1:3), that is, concerning mortals. For the Greeks say this.

And indeed the man of my peace, on whom I hoped. The 'I hoped' here is 'I took courage' concerning the man; for the Gospel also mentioned this, that this one 'the man of my peace lifted up a wing'; for they were saying that even in the fourth Psalm of Pentecost concerning him it says, 'But you, O man, my equal soul' (Ps 41:9). 'If my enemy...

He would have mocked me, or even if the one hating me had magnified himself against me, I would have been hidden from him. But you, my soul's equal—we take this regarding the one of one accord, and again 'the woman in your bosom' is your equal—'my leader and my savior'. They had as leader, not as ruler, but as my leader, running before me. And here: 'the man of my peace, in whom I hoped' (Ps 4:7).

It is nothing wonderful if you whispered against me and set a lawless word against me, if 'the man of my peace' has become the beginning of this evil of yours. Therefore he 'raised up' 'the wing', not the head 'against me'. The one eating my bread magnified a winging against me. 'The man of my peace, in whom I hoped' (Ps 4:7), 'he raised up his wing against me', he wished to wing me. It is a fluttering... and Jacob is called a winger; for he winged Esau when [he took] the blessing [of the] elder. To set upon someone with deceit is called a winging. It is someone... to lead [them] so that he might take his garment. And he who deceives toward the death of someone...

But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up, and I will repay them. Make me outside of the evils and of the bad winging of the lawless word which they set against me. These things again are said more humanly concerning the man Jesus. 'But you, Lord, have mercy, and I will repay them.' I shall be their judge. The one who rises to repay and to judge, as he finds the dispositions, gives back. Many, having experienced harm or seeing that they once condemned [him], himself is about to judge them, according to: 'they shall look upon him whom they crucified' (Jn 19:37), they come into knowledge and they know how the due retribution persists toward them.

In this I knew that you willed me. This is knowledge and proof that it is your will to have me; for in this they shall know me. The 'in this I knew' does not refer so much to his own knowledge, but rather that those of mine shall be known in this. Above all, having been condemned, will they know him?—all having received a perception of his greatness, whether they were enemies before or acquaintances. Because my enemy shall by no means be pleased with me. When I am shown as your will, when I rise and...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Meaning of Understanding
english: Let it be known that according to your will, both Judas and the devil who worked in him are able. To make them rejoice, he surrounded him with death; but upon his resurrection they do not rejoice, but rather they experience shame and stand in fear, having seen the one they had betrayed. But you took hold of me through my innocence. For I did not know sin, even though I have become sin; even though I have become a curse, I was not shown to be a curse because of a preceding sin, but so that I might loose the curse and provide a blessing. And just as it has become sin so that God might make righteous those for whom sin has become, so it has become a curse, not so that it might be held by the curse. This very thing, then, has become a curse upon a blessing, sin upon righteousness, death received for life.

Innocence, then, often signifies the absence of something, and it is when there is complete purity from sin. But when it says, 'the simple believes every word' (Ps 119:7), and also, 'bad associations corrupt good morals' (1 Cor 15:34), it speaks of the surrounding good morals. And complete virtue is also called innocence, concerning which he says, 'the simple and upright cling to me' (Ps 15:2). And you have established me before you for ever. Not for a little time, then, did I not slip, being simple before falling to enemies, but I remained simple; for 'you have established me' indeed 'for ever.' Not simply, then, but 'before you.' And not everyone who is being established is additionally established by God, but he who has the perfection established. 'He who establishes you with us in Christ.' So, you testifying to my innocence.

Blessed is the Lord God of Israel from ever and to ever (Ps 102:28). Let it be, let it be. The one having mind regarding Israel, seeing God, is a blessed God. To him I write the grace and the victory, not by our power; for even if I am simple, I do not give the whole by my innocence, but by the cooperation of God. The 'let it be, let it be' is like the 'amen' as other interpreters say. And the 'amen' is when it is taken instead of an oath; for when it says, 'truly I say to you,' Matthew and Luke write the same word, and Matthew says, 'Amen, amen, I say to you,' but Luke says, 'Truly I say to you.' Indeed, it is also said in the writings, 'Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to [your word]' (Lk 1:38).

"Your word." It is also said by those interpreting the Hebrew sounds that it means that which is believed. To the end; for understanding, to the sons of Korah, a psalm. Three sons of Korah became temple singers. And their names are brought forward in Exodus and in the Chronicles. These, just as some take from faith one soul and one heart, so also these, having received one soul from the uniting spirit which grants the singing, because of this they bring forth the verses of the psalm in unison.

And this psalm is not one filled by chance with mysteries. Because of this, "for understanding" is inscribed. Thus also in the thirty-first [Psalm] we say that it is "of the understanding to David," because he contained mysteries and riddles. And here, therefore, many riddles lie. Therefore, understanding is needed by the one encountering such psalms which are so inscribed. And just as it is necessary "to pay attention" to the "reading" of the "God-breathed Scripture," not only of the scriptures but also of "all," so also these owe to speak and to be heard with understanding.

Since, however, the name of understanding is also made clear by proximity and signifies something else in: "but understanding is good to all who practice it." Here the understanding that comes to be and is practiced is moral virtue; for especially this regulates the character of men. He says, therefore, that this psalm ought not to be spoken by voice alone, but also to be understood by the mind and to practice the works appropriate to it, according to the other meaning of understanding, about which also Paul speaks. Writing about ministry and the service toward the saints, he says: "May God grant you understanding in all things" (Eph 1:17); for he does not say understanding as the knowledge of things combined and uncombined, but the practical virtue; for who is so wise as he who has perfected his own character and regulated it? And for himself and for those speaking and those hearing? The one teaching wisely about prudence possesses the virtue of prudence himself, which also those being instructed with him possess; for this reason the right word teaches as a teacher, and especially the one of ethics, so that those hearing might become such as the speaker is. The manner which he intends is like a [light] upon the...

title: The Spiritual Deer and the Single Desire
english: As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God (Psalm 42:1). This animal is said to be a destroyer of serpents. And when it has killed the serpents, it becomes thirsty from their venom and hastens to find a spring of water, so that it may wash away the thirst and be cleansed; for it is said that as the serpents are torn apart by this animal, they cover the face of the deer with blood and other things, and so it goes away to wash itself, so that the impurity brought upon it from the destruction of the serpents may be washed away.

And something else is said about this animal: that when it grows old and sheds its antlers, it eats serpents and is renewed. The eating of serpents makes it new again. But of what kind of serpents? All the kind of venomous ones, of all the serpents or even of the whole genus. And this too: when it casts off its horns from old age, it dwells in a den until it grows horns again and becomes strong; for one without horns is vulnerable; for they are its weapons and its defenses. Therefore, when they pass through the woods, their horns are seized and thus they are torn away; so a proverb like this appears: 'Woe to deer without horns.' And this proverb alludes to this: woe to the helpless man who does not have the power to help himself.

The other thing of those signified here is shown by the saying: 'In the same way that a deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, my God' (Psalm 42:1); he compared the longing toward God to the longing of the deer for the springs; for God is a spring, and His word is a spring: 'You have left the spring of wisdom' (Job 28:12). 'For with you is the spring of life' (Psalm 36:9). And again: 'You have left me, a spring of living water,' God says (Psalm 119:172). And the Holy Spirit is a spring, if indeed all the gifts flow from Him and from Him they have their beginning.

In the same way that the sensible deer longs for the springs of water, so our soul, becoming a deer and a destroyer of harmful things, longs for you, O God. Those who 'are ready to avenge all disobedience' (Hebrews 10:29) are deer, destroying the serpents of injustice. And those having received 'authority to tread...'

The serpents and the scorpions are deer. These deer also pursue the high things. Just as they pursue the springs of waters, so too the high things; for 'mountains are the high things for the deer'. And again the same: 'He who prepares my feet like a deer' (Ps 103:6), so that having been prepared, they pursue the intelligible things.

And since I have often said that the intelligible things seem to be different and different things according to each and every different thought, even though they are the same in substance, the springs of waters which the spiritual deer seeks, and high mountains, are [the same]. Insofar as they are lifted up and given from above, they are high things; but insofar as they water and give birth to rivers in the plains, they are called springs.

Therefore, it must be said and it is morally right: the serpents are pleasures; for pleasure is diverse. And 'being led by various pleasures and desires'. He speaks concerning the faults of women whom the heterodox capture as captives. These therefore diverse deer do not long to find God; they do not seek one single desire. But one desire is the Savior and our Lord himself. Just as he is called wisdom and truth and light and righteousness, so also [he is] desire.

Furthermore, the bride in the Song of Songs, inquiring about the bridegroom, where she can find him, the doorkeepers whom she inquired of, say: 'What is your brother more excellent than your brothers, the beautiful among women?' (Song 1:9). Say [tell me] your own, the other, among the many brothers. And he says: 'My brother is white and ruddy' (Song 4:1), he is not one, he is man and God. Then, passing through his praises, he says at the end: 'His throat is sweet, all desire' (Song 4:16). His word is sweet.

You know that some desirable things are not entirely [so], but they have something unpleasant mixed in; for example, the drinking of sweet wine has something desirable. But when it is taken to excess, it works a drunkenness and is not entirely desire. Again, the sun seen is sweet. But when its flame descends, it has something unpleasant. Therefore, regarding the discourse concerning the marriage, nothing is unpleasant, it is entirely desire, it is entirely love, according to the one saying: 'My love is crucified' (Song 8:6). But the loves of others have something bitter mixed in. Just as 'all desire' is, so also 'all love' is, and for this reason the soul longs.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
